chapters.title: The Habit Loop
chapters.sourcePressure: Eugene Pauly's memory-loss case shows that procedural routines can keep running outside explicit recall; the chapter introduces cue, routine, reward as a diagnostic structure and frames automation as the brain's efficiency move.
chapters.coreMove: Split an automatic behavior into cue, routine, and reward before judging or trying to change it.
chapters.commonMisread: A weak run would write generic advice about building better habits or self-discipline, missing that this chapter is mainly a diagnostic reveal of automatic procedure.

chapters.title: The Craving Brain
chapters.sourcePressure: Claude Hopkins and Pepsodent anchor the claim that a cue gains force when the reward becomes expected; anticipation makes the loop sticky and explains why some new routines catch while others do not.
chapters.coreMove: Find the reward the cue has begun to promise in advance, then design the habit around that anticipation.
chapters.commonMisread: A weak run would treat this as another cue-routine-reward summary or as advertising trivia, instead of isolating craving as the force that energizes the loop.

chapters.title: The Golden Rule of Habit Change
chapters.sourcePressure: The golden rule says to keep the same cue and reward while changing the routine; AA and coaching examples show that substitution needs belief and support when pressure returns.
chapters.coreMove: Preserve the trigger and payoff, then install a replacement routine strong enough to survive stress.
chapters.commonMisread: A weak run would tell readers to quit bad habits through resolve, or would propose any alternative action without proving it answers the same reward.

chapters.title: Keystone Habits, or The Ballad of Paul O'Neill
chapters.sourcePressure: Paul O'Neill's worker-safety focus at Alcoa shows how one habit can force wider operational change through faster communication, accountability, and small wins.
chapters.coreMove: Choose the habit with structural spillover, not the habit that merely looks important.
chapters.commonMisread: A weak run would call any meaningful routine a keystone habit, or treat safety as a symbolic campaign rather than a lever that changed adjacent systems.

chapters.title: Starbucks and the Habit of Success
chapters.sourcePressure: Starbucks training routines show willpower becoming automatic through scripts, scenarios, and stress planning; pressure reveals defaults unless the better response has been practiced.
chapters.coreMove: Script and rehearse the first response to a stressful cue before the stressful moment arrives.
chapters.commonMisread: A weak run would praise grit or customer service politeness, missing that the chapter is about building self-control as a trained routine.

chapters.title: The Power of a Crisis
chapters.sourcePressure: Crisis is presented as the moment entrenched organizational routines become negotiable; leaders can use disruption to install new habits, but the opening is dangerous and temporary.
chapters.coreMove: Turn a breakdown into a specific new institutional routine before the system hardens around the old default.
chapters.commonMisread: A weak run would glorify crisis or write general change-management prose, instead of showing crisis as temporary leverage that still requires designed replacement habits.

chapters.title: How Target Knows What You Want Before You Do
chapters.sourcePressure: Target's use of buying patterns shows that routines become readable data; familiar placement can lower resistance to novelty, raising the ethical line between service and manipulation.
chapters.coreMove: Read the external data trail of a routine and test whether using it helps the person or quietly steers them.
chapters.commonMisread: A weak run would turn the chapter into generic privacy panic or omniscient AI prediction, missing the narrower mechanism of habit signals and familiar placement.

chapters.title: Saddleback Church and the Montgomery Bus Boycott
chapters.sourcePressure: The Montgomery bus boycott and Saddleback Church show that movements need social habits: strong ties help launch action, weak ties scale it, and peer expectations make participation repeatable.
chapters.coreMove: Build participation routines that convert private agreement into visible group expectation across strong and weak ties.
chapters.commonMisread: A weak run would attribute movements to charisma, outrage, or inspiration alone, ignoring the repeated social structure that carries participation after the spark.

chapters.title: The Neurology of Free Will
chapters.sourcePressure: Automatic routines complicate responsibility without erasing it; legal and moral tension turns on awareness, foreseeability, and whether a person could deliberately redesign or contain a risky loop.
chapters.coreMove: After a harmful loop becomes knowable, name the duty to redesign, contain, or avoid the conditions that trigger it.
chapters.commonMisread: A weak run would write a broad free-will essay or excuse all habit-driven behavior, instead of focusing on accountability once awareness and foreseeability enter.
